reconstructed_article:
The Victorian Government has approved a $380 million wind farm at Mount Gellibrand in the state's south-west. Planning Minister Rob Hulls announced the decision, describing the project as Australia's most powerful and Victoria's largest wind farm to date.

The wind farm will be located 120 km west of Melbourne, near the regional centre of Colac. It will comprise 116 turbines of the 2 MW class, with an overall capacity of 232 MW. The facility is expected to produce over 700,000 MWh annually, enough to supply approximately 132,000 Victorian households. The project is expected to create between 110 and 120 jobs during construction and up to 25 full-time positions during operation.

German company Pro Ventum International is undertaking the project. Minister Hulls acknowledged that nine objections had been lodged against the project. Local landowner Tim Gore, who plans to have 32 turbines on his property, said he was not concerned about potential noise. Pro Ventum International said it would commence work on an Environmental Management report in the coming weeks.

Wind farm critic Tim Le Roy said there was no environmental benefit from the project and that the Victorian Government would better spend its money elsewhere. In October of the previous year, Colac Otway council chief executive officer Tracey Slatter said the proposal would benefit the shire by reducing greenhouse gas emissions and addressing increasing energy demand.

reconstructed_article:
On Friday, 178 plaintiffs, including construction workers and family members of deceased workers, filed a lawsuit in Tokyo, Japan, seeking approximately 6.6 billion yen (about 64 million USD) in damages from the Japanese government and 46 building manufacturers. Reports indicate this is the first class action in Japan related to health damages caused by asbestos exposure at construction sites. The plaintiffs are from Tokyo and surrounding areas.

They claim the government and manufacturers were aware of the dangers of asbestos inhalation but did not take adequate precautions, including ceasing to promote asbestos as a cheap construction material and banning its production. After inhaling asbestos in the workplace, 172 people developed lung cancer or mesothelioma, and nearly half of those afflicted have died.

Plaintiffs argue that the government and health ministry did not act swiftly enough after international organizations issued warnings in 1972 that asbestos could be a carcinogen. They also cite the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry for sanctioning asbestos use under the Factory Act, and the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism for authorizing asbestos-containing materials under Japan's Building Standards Law.

Approximately 40 construction workers plan to file a similar lawsuit in June. Following a 2005 revelation that residents near a factory developed asbestos-related diseases, the government implemented a 2006 law providing relief to victims and relatives. Plaintiffs argue the assistance is insufficient. Japan banned the spraying of asbestos in 1975.

reconstructed_article: New Jersey school officials acted on Friday after the discovery of airborne asbestos in Renaissance Middle School in Montclair, New Jersey, prompting the evacuation of over 200 students and the school's closure. The school, part of Montclair Public Schools, was closed Monday and remained closed Tuesday while undergoing asbestos testing and cleaning. According to a letter sent to parents by the Superintendent's Office of Montclair Public Schools, plaster may have been disturbed during construction on new fire doors on Thursday. An inspection arranged by the school district indicated asbestos was present in the plaster, and a subsequent inspection by asbestos consultant Detail Associates revealed airborne asbestos fiber levels exceeding the acceptable range in the third floor hallway. Business administrator Dana Sullivan stated that testing on March 31 confirmed asbestos in a brown undercoating of plaster. The affected area was sealed off by district officials. Public Information Officer Laura Federico said sixth and seventh graders were transported to Hillside Elementary School and eighth graders to another location. Detail Associates conducted cleaning on Saturday. At a Monday meeting between parents and district officials, parents demanded lockers be included in cleanup, prompting Tuesday's closure. Steve Jaraczewski of Detail Associates said one of four test samples was positive for airborne asbestos at over six times acceptable levels. He criticized the asbestos management plan provided by the Archdiocese of Newark, which owns the building. Archdiocese representative Jim Goodness stated the building would reopen soon. The state Department of Environmental Protection is supervising the cleanup.

The commitment was made in Thailand at Asia's first ministerial conference on tiger conservation. The thirteen countries that endorsed the pledge were Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, China, India, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, Nepal, Russia, Thailand, and Vietnam, all countries where the wild Asian tiger is still found. Thai Prime Minister Abhisit Vejjajiva stated in a video address that the wild tiger is in crisis and that this may be the last chance to save it. The meeting was partially organized by the Global Tiger Initiative, a coalition within the World Bank, as well as the Smithsonian Institution and various conservation groups. Meeting host Suwit Khunkitti, Thailand's minister of natural resources and environment, noted that there were 100,000 tigers across range countries 100 years ago, compared to about 3,500 today. According to the World Wildlife Fund (WWF), tiger numbers have declined due to poaching. The animals live in only seven percent of the territory they occupied a hundred years ago, according to Voice of America. WWF representative Michael Baltzer said it was important to act during the Year of the Tiger. Global Tiger Initiative program director Keshav Varma said saving the tiger also preserves habitat for other species and draws attention to issues including encroachment and corruption.

Campbell also said development of a viable degradable bag to replace existing lightweight plastic ones is key to further reductions. reconstructed_article:
The Australian Government is building a $210 million, 800-bed detention facility on Christmas Island, 1400km off Australia's northwest coast. Construction began in January 2005, and the facility is scheduled to be operational by late 2006. A DIMIA spokesperson confirmed it would serve as an immigration reception and processing centre and that a considered review of mainland detention centres would likely follow its completion.

Christmas Island Shire President Gordon Thompson said residents were concerned about impacts on tourism, restricted access to fishing and snorkelling areas, and lack of consultation. He said the Shire council was not notified when the existing Christmas Island detention centre reopened on November 17 to detain seven West Timorese asylum seekers. Azmi Yon, president of the island's Malay association, said locals sought written clarification on the facility's purpose.

Democrats senator Andrew Bartlett claimed transferring asylum seekers to the remote location denied them proper processing and legal access. Greens senator Kerry Nettle called for construction to be suspended, citing existing detention capacity of 3,975 people across facilities including Baxter, Villawood, Maribyrnong, Perth, Port Augusta, Port Hedland, and Woomera.

Environmental concerns were raised because the site is adjacent to Abbott's Booby habitat within Christmas Island National Park. Research indicated nesting birds within 300 metres of clearings experienced lower breeding success, with 36% of breeding sites in that zone. The Wilderness Society criticised the government's self-exemption from EPBC Act environmental scrutiny.

The manufacturing fault could lead to an elevated risk of fatigue crack initiation and growth, oil leakage, and a resulting oil fire. The agency urged Rolls-Royce to address the safety issue and take actions necessary to ensure the safety of flight operations in aircraft equipped with Trent 900 series engines. Qantas grounded all six of its A380 fleet for safety checks before returning them to service. Qantas stated there was no immediate risk to flight safety but would conduct further investigations. Two A380 aircraft were in operational service, with both to be inspected at the Qantas Jet Base in Sydney. Lufthansa and Singapore Airlines also use A380 aircraft with Trent engines. Singapore Airlines said it was checking its A380 engines on a daily basis and would carry out the new ATSB-advised checks as quickly as possible. The A380 made its first commercial flight in 2007 and has a maximum capacity of 840 passengers, though Qantas' aircraft can carry 450.

Business Secretary Peter Mandelson said it is essential that Corus does everything it can legally, and with the government's assistance, to reinstate the agreement. Mandelson also said the government was not prepared to reconcile itself to the inevitable closure of the plant. Liberal Democrats including Simon Hughes, Fiona Hall, and Stephen Hughes MEP supported the idea that the government should subsidise wages at the plant on a temporary basis. The leader of Redcar and Cleveland Council, Councillor George Dunning, described the announcement as being hit by a mini earthquake. Adams said the move could bring to an end a heritage of steelmaking at Teesside. Corus said a 90-day consultation period is due to begin. reconstructed_article:
Bach Technology unveiled MusicDNA at the end of January. The new music file format, designed as a replacement for MP3, uses similar compression methods but adds an XML file containing additional content such as lyrics, artwork, tour dates, blog posts, videos, and Twitter feeds. The files also include audio analysis information intended to improve search, recommendation, and playlist tools.

CEO Stefan Kohlmeyer stated that MusicDNA has been in development since the company was founded in 2007. Bach Technology holds a strategic partnership with Fraunhofer IDMT, whose CEO Karlheinz Brandenburg—credited with inventing the MP3—participates in research and development discussions at Bach.

Unlike iTunes LP, MusicDNA is built on open standards and is platform-agnostic, allowing transfer between devices and the purchase of individual tracks rather than complete albums. Additional content updates dynamically when the user is online, but only paid files receive these updates. Bach Technology describes this as an incentive to purchase legitimate files rather than use peer-to-peer networks.

Mark Mulligan, vice president and research director at Forrester Research, told a UK newspaper that innovations like iTunes LP need to go further, suggesting people should pay once for regularly updated content.

Kohlmeyer noted that MP3 was developed over twenty years ago and does not add to the listening experience beyond portability.

The MusicDNA rollout is staggered over 2010, with beta versions expected around Easter and full commercial rollout expected in summer.

The Taiwan External Trade Development Council (TAITRA) announced the winners of the Gold and Silver Awards on Thursday at the 2008 16th-annual Taiwan Excellence Awards, held at the Taipei International Convention Center. TAITRA organized the event to promote products made in Taiwan.

This year, 601 products competed for eight gold medals and twenty-one silver awards. In the ICT category, 388 products from the industry were on display. In total, 308 products from 102 companies were named "Taiwan Excellent Products." Several world-class experts judged the nominated products and selected the final twenty-nine winners based on four critical factors. TAITRA also included categories in which people could vote over the Internet or by using their mobile phones.

ASUSTeK Computer Incorporated won two Gold Awards and six Silver Awards and was the biggest winner. The ASUS Eee PC 4G, which has features including mobility, reliability, and connectivity, won a Gold Award and was voted "Most Popular Product" by Internet and mobile users. ASUSTeK Computer Incorporated received the Taiwan Excellence Best Performance Award, while D-Link Corporation received the Taiwan Excellence Achievement Award.

Gold Award winners included the ASUS R700t portable navigation device, the AverVision SPB350, the N133I6 ultra-slim wide LCD panel, the MBA-00 Glee Cube multimedia IP-TV box, the P3650 Touch Cruise, the Hiwin E2 ecological and economical lubrication module, and the Merida Ninety Six carbon full suspension. Silver Award winners included products from ASUS, Gigabyte, Panasonic, D-Link, ZyXEL, Giant, and others across multiple categories.

reconstructed_article: L. Alan Winters, distinguished professor of economics at the University of Sussex and founding director of the UK Trade Policy Observatory (UKTPO), was interviewed about UK trade policy following Brexit. Winters stated he was opposed to Brexit and considers it poor economic policy, arguing the UK would have been better off with a tighter relationship with Europe to keep trade costs lower. He co-authored reports including "The Costs of Brexit," "COVID-19 will reinforce the Brexit shock," and "Taking stock of the new UK-EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement." Winters said Brexit and COVID-19 shocks interact, making recovery from lost export markets harder. He dismissed the idea that trade with distant partners like Australia, New Zealand, or CPTPP members could replace EU trade, noting the EU represents approximately half of UK trade and that benefits of trade agreements weaken with distance. On fishing, he noted the UK gained some quota transfer but must still prove compliance with EU standards to sell fish in Europe. He criticized government statistics presenting 218 billion in rolled-over trade as new income. Regarding the Northern Ireland Protocol, he attributed complications to Brexit and the specific form of Brexit chosen by Boris Johnson. Winters argued the UK should pursue a quiet, cooperative role in the WTO and urged the G7 to focus on repairing the multilateral trading system rather than pursuing bilateral photo opportunities. He expressed concern about rising Chinese-Western tensions and cautioned against framing democratic cooperation in an anti-China light. He called for greater domestic debate on trade policy, noting the executive faces few constraints.

reconstructed_article: Roger D. Kornberg of the United States won the 2006 Nobel Prize for chemistry for his studies of the molecular basis of eukaryotic transcription. His work explains how information encoded in DNA is used to produce the proteins that keep cells functioning. Eukaryotes are multi-celled organisms, such as animals, plants and fungi, which have their genetic material stored in nuclei within their cells. To use their genetic information, eukaryotes extract bits of the coded information via the formation of messenger RNA, which consists of copies of a particular gene within the DNA strand. Translation takes place when proteins are built from the information transcribed with the messenger RNA. Eukaryotic transcription is vital for life. If transcription is interrupted, as can happen when cells are exposed to certain toxins, the cells will die. Kornberg documented eukaryotic transcription with snapshots of the process in action. He created the snapshots by crystallizing cellular material partway through transcription and exposing them to x-rays that produced patterns revealing the intermediate structures. His work may lead to novel drugs and medical treatments. Kornberg's father Arthur Kornberg won the Nobel Prize in physiology and medicine in 1959 for explaining how organisms synthesize DNA from nucleotides.

The ATSB said the manufacturing fault could lead to an elevated risk of fatigue crack initiation and growth, oil leakage, and a resulting oil fire. The agency urged Rolls-Royce to address the safety issue and take actions necessary to ensure the safety of flight operations in aircraft equipped with Trent 900 series engines. Singapore Airlines said it was checking its A380 engines on a daily basis and would carry out the new ATSB-advised checks as quickly as possible. The A380 made its first commercial flight in 2007 and has a maximum capacity of 840 passengers, though Qantas' can carry 450.

reconstructed_article: George Smoot of the United States and John Mather of NASA shared the 2006 Nobel Prize in Physics for their discovery of the blackbody form and anisotropy of the cosmic microwave background radiation. The Nobel Prize Committee cited the physicists for their work on the Cosmic Background Explorer (COBE) project. COBE revealed faint fluctuations in microwave signals from space that are thought to be remnants of the Big Bang. Although the precise origin of the fluctuations in the cosmic microwave background is not yet clear, they may represent clumps in the very early universe that led to the galaxies seen today. Prior to the COBE map of the universe, it was unclear why the universe contained stars and galaxies rather than an evenly distributed dust cloud. Theorists had predicted that a sensitive measurement of microwaves from the sky would reveal minute temperature fluctuations, which represent variations in the density of matter in the early universe. The denser portions served as seeds for galaxies that formed later. COBE was the first experiment sensitive enough to confirm the predicted temperature variations encoded in the map of the microwave background. The initial discovery of the Cosmic Microwave Background by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson led to their award of the 1978 Nobel Prize in physics. Although they measured the approximate temperature of the universe to be about 3.5 kelvins, their ground-based microwave telescope could not pick out the detail available to COBE.

The Scottish Government has confirmed that an adult with underlying health problems died on Friday from the H1N1 virus, bringing the total number of deaths from the virus in Scotland to 40. The victim, who contracted the virus, remains unidentified.

Nicola Sturgeon, the current Health Secretary in Scotland, stated that people with underlying health conditions are at greater risk of complications. She said the vaccine is being prioritised for this group. Vaccinations are being administered as vaccines arrive in the country, and those who accept the invitation will be vaccinated by Christmas.

The announcement came one day after the Scottish Government set out its plan for healthy children between the ages of five months and six years to receive a jab to prevent swine flu. Around 260,000 children are to receive the jab.

Sturgeon said the decision was made in line with independent scientific advice from the Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation (JCVI). She stated that JCVI advice has guided all decisions around the vaccination programme. According to JCVI advice, young children are more at risk of contracting the virus, and the highest rate of hospitalisations has been in the under-five age group.

Sturgeon noted that the vast majority of young children, like the rest of the population, have mild symptoms and recover relatively quickly. She said the Scottish Government's aim is to ensure young children are fully protected against the virus.

reconstructed_article: Matthew Wright, host of British television programme The Wright Stuff, apologised for remarks made on the show regarding the murder of Liam Aitchison. During the edition broadcast on Tuesday, Wright said "there's been another murder" in a false Scottish accent, referencing the UK television crime drama Taggart. Panelist Charlie Baker remarked the investigation would be like "the longest episode of Taggart of all time," and the audience laughed. Liam Aitchison's family issued a statement calling the comments "insensitive and offensive" and "very upsetting and insulting for, not just the family, but for the whole community of the Western Isles." His father, Norman Aitchison, wrote on the programme's website that he was "disgusted" and asked whether panel members would joke if it were their own child. On the following day's broadcast, Wright said he would "like to apologise" if viewers were offended, stating there was no intention to belittle the tragedy. Channel 5's spokeswoman said Wright's apology was "clear." Wright said he had not been helped by campaigns urging people to report him to Ofcom, a UK media regulator, and advised such people to "grow up." Channel 5 removed Tuesday's episode from its website. Angus MacNeil, MP for Na h-Eileanan an Iar, described Wright's behaviour as "beyond belief" and intended to complain to Ofcom. Comhairle nan Eilean Siar also complained. A Facebook page titled "Report The Wright Stuff to Ofcom" attracted over two thousand likes. Ofcom was assessing complaints but had not decided whether to investigate.

U.S. District Judge Stein ruled that the use of a 25-second clip from John Lennon's song "Imagine" in the film "Expelled" is likely defensible under the fair use doctrine. "Expelled," produced by Premise Media and starring comedian Ben Stein, is a film critical of religion and a documentary claiming that intelligent design proponents are being suppressed by the scientific community. The film uses the clip to represent what Premise representative Anthony Falzone described at a hearing as "the most popular and persuasive embodiment of this viewpoint that the world is better off without religion." In the song, Lennon proposes the hypothetical "Imagine there's no heaven ... and no religion too."

On April 23, 2008, Lennon's widow, Yoko Ono, along with his sons Sean and Julian, and music producer EMI Blackwood, Inc., filed suit against Premise Media seeking damages for alleged copyright infringement, as the song had not been licensed for use in the film. On May 19, a preliminary injunction was issued preventing distribution of the film. On June 2, Judge Stein ruled that the fair use defense Premise Media raised would likely succeed and lifted the injunction, writing that "the fair use of a copyrighted work for the purposes of criticism and commentary is not an infringement of copyright."

Premise Media has also faced copyright claims over animated sequences resembling "The Inner Life of the Cell," produced by XVIVO and Harvard University. Ono stated that "it is a pity that this decision weakens the rights of all copyright owners" and plans to appeal.

reconstructed_article: On Thursday, the U.S. House of Representatives voted 269-152 to reject the Net Neutrality Amendment to the COPE Act. The House then advanced the COPE Act, passing it by a 321-101 vote the same day. The act was designed to make it easier for telecommunications companies to offer cable TV service and strengthen competition. Proponents said it would lower high-speed Internet prices by enabling providers to bundle phone, data, video, and mobile services. It was the first major telecommunications bill before Congress in over a decade. The Net Neutrality amendment sought to require broadband providers to treat all data equally, specifying a duty not to block, impair, degrade, discriminate against, or interfere with access to lawful content, applications, or services. Its passage would have prevented companies such as AT&T, Verizon, and Comcast from charging content providers like Google, Yahoo, Amazon, or eBay for priority network access. Democrats largely supported the amendment, with 140 voting in favor and 58 against, while 11 Republicans voted for it and 211 against. House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi argued that additional fees would burden small web-based businesses and hamper noncommercial communications. Phone companies and Congressional allies argued the restrictions would discourage investment in network upgrades. The bill is due to be discussed next in the Senate.

reconstructed_article: On Tuesday at approximately 4:00 a.m., around 500 melon-headed whales were spotted swimming near the shores of Pilar, Bataan, approximately 135 kilometers northwest of Manila. Philippine Coast Guard commander Luis Tuazon and Bataan Governor Enrique Garcia Jr. mobilized in response to the sighting and coordinated an effort to protect the animals. Authorities deployed more than 100 fishermen and volunteers, along with personnel from the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR), local police, and the Coast Guard. They used dozens of fishing boats with engines shut off to guide the whales toward deeper waters by clapping and hitting the water surface. The mammals were initially misidentified as dolphins but were later identified as melon-headed whales by local veterinarian Mariel Flores. Four dead whales were found in Abucay and Tortugas, including two adult females, one pregnant and one that had given birth to a calf that also died. A necropsy by Dr. Lemnuel Aragones of the University of the Philippines found the two adults had damaged eardrums. Provincial veterinarian Alberto Venturina said the adults weighed 250 to 300 kilograms, and the calf was approximately one month old. BFAR director Malcolm Sarmiento Jr. noted this was the largest stranding recorded, with previous events involving only 20 to 30 animals. By 4:30 p.m., authorities and volunteers had guided the whales back to deeper waters. edit_plan.after: On Thursday, the U.S. House of Representatives voted 269-152 to reject the Net Neutrality Amendment to the COPE Act. The amendment sought to require broadband providers to treat all data equally, specifying a duty not to block, impair, degrade, discriminate against, or interfere with access to lawful content, applications, or services. Its passage would have prevented companies such as AT&T, Verizon, and Comcast from charging content providers like Google, Yahoo, Amazon, or eBay for priority network access. House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi argued that additional fees would burden small web-based businesses and hamper noncommercial communications. Phone companies and Congressional allies argued the restrictions would discourage investment in network upgrades. Democrats largely supported the amendment, with 140 voting in favor and 58 against, while 11 Republicans voted for it and 211 against. The COPE Act, designed to make it easier for telecommunications companies to offer cable TV service and strengthen competition, passed by a 321-101 vote the same day. Proponents said it would lower high-speed Internet prices by enabling providers to bundle phone, data, video, and mobile services. It was the first major telecommunications bill before Congress in over a decade.

They made the commitment in Thailand at Asia's first ministerial conference on tiger conservation. The thirteen countries that endorsed the pledge were Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, China, India, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, Nepal, Russia, Thailand, and Vietnam, all countries where the wild Asian tiger is still found. In a video address, Thai Prime Minister Abhisit Vejjajiva stated that the wild tiger is in crisis and that this may be the last chance to save it. The Global Tiger Initiative, a coalition within the World Bank, the Smithsonian Institution, and various conservation groups partially organized the meeting. Meeting host Suwit Khunkitti, Thailand's minister of natural resources and environment, noted that there were 100,000 tigers across range countries 100 years ago, compared to about 3,500 today. According to the World Wildlife Fund (WWF), tiger numbers have declined due to poaching. According to Voice of America, the animals live in only seven percent of the territory they occupied a hundred years ago. WWF representative Michael Baltzer said it was important to act during the Year of the Tiger. Global Tiger Initiative program director Keshav Varma said saving the tiger also preserves habitat for other species and draws attention to issues including encroachment and corruption.

Police in Purcell, Oklahoma, about 40 miles (64 km) south of Oklahoma City, discovered the body of ten-year-old Jamie Rose Bolin on Friday in the apartment of Kevin Underwood, 26, a resident of the same apartment complex. McClain County District Attorney Tim Kuykendall said the body was found in a storage bin in the bedroom closet. Underwood was arrested on suspicion of first-degree murder and held without bail pending further proceedings. He had no known prior criminal record or history of mental illness.

Bolin was last seen on Wednesday near the Purcell public library, and her family reported her missing that night. Officials issued an Amber Alert on Thursday night, noting that no abduction had been reported initially. Underwood came under suspicion at an information checkpoint set up at the apartment complex.

Police found a decorative dagger, hacksaw, barbecue skewers, meat tenderizer, and wooden cutting board in his apartment. Preliminary autopsy reports indicated Bolin died of asphyxiation and blunt force trauma to the head. Authorities said deep saw marks on the body suggested an attempt to decapitate her. Police suspected possible postmortem molestation, as the body was found unclothed.

Purcell Police Chief David Tompkins stated the motive appeared to involve a plan to kidnap, rape, torture, kill, decapitate, drain of blood, rape the corpse, eat the corpse, and dispose of the organs and bones. Corus, the world's fifth largest steel producer, announced on Friday that its steelworks in Teesside, England, may be mothballed, threatening the jobs of 1,920 employees. The closure of Corus' Teesside operations may be forced by a consortium's refusal to honour a 10-year contract with Corus' Teesside Cast Products, which accounted for 78% of the plant's operations.

The leader of Redcar and Cleveland Council, Councillor George Dunning, described the announcement as being hit by a mini earthquake.

Liberal Democrats including Simon Hughes, Fiona Hall, and Stephen Hughes MEP supported the idea that the government should subsidise wages at the plant on a temporary basis. Hughes and Hall suggested the government should apply to the EU's European Globalisation Fund.

A 90-day consultation period is due to begin, Corus said.

Atlanta, Georgia lost its bid to host Wikimania 2008, which was awarded to Alexandria, Egypt. The selection prompted discussion on public mailing lists regarding safety, free speech, and the jury's decision process. After the loss, organizers began planning a Conference of the Americas focused on Wikimedia in the Americas.

One organizer, an unpaid intern at the Wikimedia Foundation offices in St. Petersburg, Florida, stated that planning discussions began before the Wikimania location was announced. He said the conference was not created in retaliation or to compete with Wikimania, and that its goal is to provide a Wikimedia event for the western hemisphere, noting that travel to Egypt is more expensive for people in the region.

The conference is scheduled for May 15-18, 2008, at the Georgia Institute of Technology in Atlanta. It will cover Wikimedia and the free culture movement in relation to communities in North America, including the United States and Canada, and Latin America. A journalism segment will be held at the Turner Broadcasting building on Techwood Drive in Midtown Atlanta.

Over 100 interested parties across the United States have expressed interest in volunteering or attending. The Wikimedia Foundation and Wikimedia Argentina have received proposals for endorsement, with decisions pending. Georgia Tech, the Public Journalism Network, and the Carolina Open Source Initiative sponsor the conference.

The report mentions India over 300 times, compared with 48 mentions of Spain, 22 of Canada, and 15 of New Zealand. The World Bank states in the report that gender equality contributes to productivity, outcomes for the next generation, and representative decision making. In India, improved local-level gender equality correlated with improvements in sanitation, water supplies, irrigation, and schools. Nationally, a woman’s income correlated positively with years her children spent in school. No gender gap exists in attendance for the richest 20% of Indian families, but males outnumber females 5 to 1 among the poorest 20%. Girls in the bottom 20% average completion of Grade 1; males average Grade 6. By age 15, parents in Andhra Pradesh prioritize outcomes for male children over female ones. Indian women earn $0.64 for every $1 earned by men, compared with $0.62 in Germany, $0.60 in Georgia, $0.90 in Malawi, $0.82 in Egypt, and $0.80 in Benin and Mexico. A fifth of married Indian women do not control household spending decisions, an 18% average matching Mozambique, between Nigeria at 14% and Zambia and Rwanda at 20%. India reduced average children per woman from six to three in 35 years, compared with 100 years in the United States. India’s maternal mortality rate is six times that of Sri Lanka. Excess female deaths in India dropped by 8,000, from 265,000 in 1990 to 257,000 in 2008; in China, excess female deaths grew by 202,000.

reconstructed_article:
U.S. District Judge Stein ruled that the use of a 25-second clip from John Lennon's song "Imagine" in a film critical of religion is likely defensible under the fair use doctrine. The film "Expelled," produced by Premise Media and starring comedian Ben Stein, deploys the clip to represent what Premise representative Anthony Falzone described at a hearing as "the most popular and persuasive embodiment of this viewpoint that the world is better off without religion." In the song, Lennon proposes the hypothetical "Imagine there's no heaven ... and no religion too."

On April 23, 2008, Lennon's widow, Yoko Ono, along with his sons Sean and Julian, and music producer EMI Blackwood, Inc., filed suit against Premise Media seeking substantial damages for alleged copyright infringement, as the song had not been licensed for use in the film. On May 19, a preliminary injunction was issued preventing distribution of the film. On June 2, Judge Stein ruled that the fair use defense would likely succeed and lifted the injunction, writing that "the fair use of a copyrighted work for the purposes of criticism and commentary is not an infringement of copyright."

"Expelled" is a documentary claiming that intelligent design proponents are being suppressed by the scientific community. It has received sharp criticism from scientists and film critics and has faced additional copyright claims over animated sequences resembling "The Inner Life of the Cell," produced by XVIVO and Harvard University. Ono said that "it is a pity that this decision weakens the rights of all copyright owners" and plans to appeal.
